frames.narration: A campaign to 600 addresses starts. The app sends one message, for ann@gmail.com, to the Send API.
Before accepting it, the API asks the suppression list whether ann has ever hard bounced or complained. She has not, so the message is stored durably and accepted.
The message goes on the queue for gmail.com. This queue is allowed 30 messages a minute from this sender, while the small tiny.org queue is allowed only 3, so neither holds up the other.

When its turn comes, the signing step adds a DKIM signature over the headers and body. The domain's SPF record already lists the sending IP, and its DMARC policy asks receivers to reject mail that fails both.
The MTA sends it from an IP in the warmed-up pool. Gmail answers 451, a temporary failure. That is a deferral, not a failure, so the message is not dropped and the address is not suppressed.

The message goes back on its queue with a delay of 2 minutes, and a longer one after a second failure (4, then 8, then 16). Waiting is also what the receiver asked for, and a quick retry would count against the sender's reputation.
Two minutes later the second attempt is accepted with 250. The message has now been delivered once, and the result is recorded at once so a crash does not send it again.

Another address in the campaign, bob@tiny.org, does not exist. The server answers 550, a permanent failure. The bounce processor adds bob to the suppression list, so he is never mailed again, and the bad address costs only one send.
Ann replies. The sender's server delivers the reply to our inbound SMTP, which checks the IP against blocklists, SPF and DKIM before it accepts the message.

The spam filter scores the message as very unlikely to be spam, so it goes to the inbox. The body is saved once in the mailbox store and the user's metadata row points to it. The search index receives it through a queue and has it indexed a couple of seconds later.
